itera.description: A subscription course platform with a synchronous “Live class” mode: the instructor advances the whole cohort in real time, with a shared timer, raise-hand, ranking and podium. A five-app ecosystem — student player, authoring MCP, contract package, API and documentation.
itera.longDescription: ITERA is a subscription course platform built as a five-app ecosystem, on its own Supabase, with RLS as the authorization authority — there is no service_role key anywhere in the servers. The learner-facing player is a Vite + React 18 SPA with Monaco, TanStack Query, PT/EN i18n and 59 test files across Vitest, Playwright and Storybook. itera-mcp is a Streamable-HTTP MCP server in Fastify exposing 21 authoring tools (Program → Unit → Lesson → Activity), where every write is validated against the author's JWT and gated by RLS policies. The Zod package @iterahq/activity-spec is the single source of truth for the 11 activity kinds, collapsing a drift that used to live in three places — the database enum, the player's type union and the MCP's constant — so an activity is validated identically on the server and on the client. itera-api is a pull-only REST v1 in Express + Zod, with per-tenant API keys, keyset pagination, federated SSO via token exchange, and Stripe billing. The landing page and the documentation live in an Astro + Starlight turborepo sharing one brand-token package. The hardest feature is the live class: a single private Supabase Realtime channel, protected by RLS, carries three concerns at once — broadcast for the instant cohort-wide advance, postgres_changes as the durable truth for anyone reconnecting mid-class, and presence for the roster of who is in the room. On top of that run a per-activity synchronized timer with add-time, raise-hand, a top-three podium, a ranking, a "who's done" view scoped to who is actually present, and the class stage: the instructor pulls a learner's in-progress work — not just the finished answer — and the cohort watches the code being typed live, with the instructor able to solve their own activity right there in front of everyone. Login is passwordless, by OTP code or magic link, because asking a teenager for a password in their first class is losing the class. The code exercise is graded deterministically, tolerant of whitespace and accents, and the learner can restart from the starter code or recover whatever they were writing after a reload. The most recent addition is BYOC: the activity is generated from the learner's own context, so the exercise speaks the language of whoever is solving it. Attendance and answers — both correct and incorrect — are persisted and become the post-class report, aggregated in TypeScript rather than in the database. Nothing the learner needs comes from a public CDN: Monaco and the fonts are served from our own domain, because the class runs on school and community networks where a blocked CDN is a realistic scenario. That decision was validated in practice: the platform ran a live, free programming pilot class for teenagers at Instituto Educar+.

deck.description: A personal command center for working with AI agents directly on my VPS. It brings together agent chat, real multi-device terminals, persistent memory, scheduled prompts, a financial ledger, a live code bench, a knowledge graph and host administration in a single web interface. Built alone, from scratch.
deck.longDescription: Deck is the platform I built — alone, from scratch — to be my command center when working with AI agents running on my own VPS. Instead of being stuck in an SSH terminal, Deck wires the browser straight to the machine: each session opens a Claude agent with isolated context, and I watch the execution in real time. The chat surfaces the reasoning, the tools, the agent's task list in a tray pinned above the composer, and the cost of every turn in tokens, time and money — including turns run straight from the terminal, reconstructed from history. Long sessions load only recent messages, with a button that pulls in whatever came before a /compact. The terminals are real VPS PTYs inside the app, with tabs and state shared across devices: the same terminal is still alive if I open it from my phone. Around the chat sit the areas that cover the whole operation. Contexts is the agent's persistent memory in read mode — typed markdown files (user, project, feedback, reference) that it writes on its own and consults between conversations. Skills is the catalogue of abilities the agent loads on demand. Crons are scheduled prompts that fire autonomous turns at the appointed time, with nobody in front of the screen. Points is a financial ledger: the agent records its own score when it finishes a task, and the route cross-references that with the project tree and the invoices pulled from the DevFellowship API, with a configurable value per point. Playground is a code bench with live preview across several runtimes — React, HTML, an iPhone frame, SVG and a test judge — plus snippet sharing by link. Graph builds a knowledge graph of the code with tree-sitter, 100% locally. Usage is the consumption observatory: estimated cost, tokens and turns per session, plus the plan's rate-limit window. Admin & Host exposes VPS health and inventory (CPU, RAM, load, disk, uptime, CLIs on PATH, MCP servers, tmux sessions, plugins) with sensitive actions behind a confirmation and an admin role on the relay. Notes is a markdown scratchpad with autosave, and the in-app documentation explains every part. Architecture: React + TypeScript + Vite front end on Vercel, a Node WebSocket backend on a Hetzner VPS, session orchestration through tmux, integration with the Claude API and with MCP servers (Supabase, Infisical and my own), persistence in Supabase and secrets in Infisical. It all runs on its own design system, with primitives and a living gallery at /ds. Designed, architected and implemented by me.

paymentsApp.description: DevFellowship's revenue pipeline, from contract to fiscal invoice: it generates the document, collects the e-signature on Autentique, schedules the recurring billing, issues the Pix through Woovi and the NFS-e through Spedy — with a dunning layer, reconciliation and a cron dispatcher on top. Production software moving real money.
paymentsApp.longDescription: DFL Payments started as a remote invoices micro-frontend in the Module Federation ecosystem and grew into DevFellowship's entire revenue pipeline. The original flow is still there: the fellow selects the reference month and the responsible organization, the system lists the deliveries whose tasks are all completed and computes points × rate to close the invoice amount automatically. On top of that the B2B pipeline was built. A contract defines amount, billing mode and recurrence; from it the system generates the document from a template, sends it for e-signature on Autentique and, when the signature webhook comes back, activates the contract and materializes the installment schedule. A cron dispatcher wakes each installment on the right date and moves it through the status kanban — scheduled, awaiting invoice, dispatched, awaiting Pix, paid, overdue or cancelled. The Pix is generated by Woovi and confirmation arrives by webhook with HMAC signature verification on the server. The service invoice is issued automatically through the Spedy API, with the NFS-e status returning by webhook and tied to the charge that originated it. Closing the loop are a dunning ladder for delinquency, a reconciliation screen between what was charged and what actually landed, contract addenda that change only future installments without rewriting the past, and a revenue forecast. The sensitive logic lives in tested TypeScript — billing, schedule, recurrence and forecast services have unit tests — rather than in database procedures, keeping the database thin and authorization in RLS.

ciRevisorBot.description: CI bot running on GitHub Actions. Executes build, tests, lint and architecture checks — then posts inline comments and summary on the PR via Claude API.
ciRevisorBot.longDescription: DFL-Bot Reviewer is the shared CI system across all DevFellowship repos. Each PR triggers: build, Vitest, verify docs, lint, architecture checks, typecheck. Then the bot runs two steps: Inline review (analyzes the diff via Claude API and posts comments on changed lines) and Summary comment (consolidates the result on the PR). Example: 'Review submitted: 3 new inline comment(s), 0 file-level item(s)'. Based on DFL CI core, a reusable composite action.

altpay.description: On-chain microcredit for rideshare drivers: an in-house score with no credit-bureau lookup, instant credit and Pix collections. Won the Chainlink track at the hackathon (Solana + Chainlink CRE/CCIP).
altpay.longDescription: AltPay (Uber Money) is a microcredit platform for rideshare drivers. The driver connects a wallet and declares their profile in an onboarding flow that never queries a credit bureau ("you declare, we adjust"), and the system computes an in-house score that decides approval, limit and interest rate. The credit lands via Pix in seconds, and collections are issued and tracked through Woovi. The credit decision runs on-chain: the score is decided on the DON through Chainlink CRE and written on-chain via CCIP, with disbursement and repayment settled by a Solana program built with Anchor. I worked on the front end, the backend (Supabase Edge Functions) and the on-chain integration (Solana + Chainlink). The project won the Chainlink track at the hackathon.

valdez.description: Discord bot in TypeScript that lives inside the voice channel: it joins on its own when someone shows up, tracks hours in call with a leaderboard, records a replay of the last few minutes and plays music from YouTube and Spotify. Runs on a Hetzner VPS with healthcheck, self-healing and OOM protection.
valdez.longDescription: Valdez is a Discord bot written in TypeScript on top of discord.js 14 and @discordjs/voice, designed to live inside the server's voice channel. Presence is automatic by occupancy: it joins when the first human arrives and leaves when the call empties. Every join and leave becomes a session persisted in SQLite (better-sqlite3 in WAL mode), which feeds /horas and /leaderboard with the call-time ranking. The hardest feature is the replay buffer: the bot subscribes to the voice receiver and keeps a sliding window of the last few minutes of Opus packets per user in memory, pruned periodically so audio from someone who spoke and then went quiet doesn't pile up — on /replay those packets are decoded to PCM, mixed by timeline (rather than simply concatenated, which was the cause of the stuttering audio) and exported to MP3 via ffmpeg. There is also a music player with a queue, loop, a persistent modal with control buttons and YouTube search via yt-dlp, with support for Spotify playlists and albums. The part that taught me the most was operations: the bot migrated from Fly.io to a Hetzner VPS on Docker Compose and gained a real resilience layer — a /health endpoint reporting gateway and voice-connection state, autoheal restarting the container when the healthcheck fails, memory limits with oom_score_adj and swap, an external heartbeat acting as a dead-man's switch, uncaughtException and unhandledRejection handlers, and DNS resolution forced to IPv4 after investigating voice disconnects through the closeCode.
